entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Cacciaguida degli Elisei, a Florentine knight and crusader who died in 1148, holds his primary historical significance not from his direct actions, but as the great-great-grandfather and revered ancestral figure of the poet Dante Alighieri. A member of the noble Elisei family, Cacciaguida's life, though sparsely documented outside of his literary afterlife, embodies the martial and pious ideals of the High Middle Ages, serving as a vital link between Dante's contemporary Florence and its perceived heroic past.

His known historical activities center on his participation in the Second Crusade (1147-1149), likely responding to Pope Eugenius III's call to defend the Latin East after the fall of Edessa. Cacciaguida was knighted by Emperor Conrad III, a key leader of the crusade, signifying his status and commitment. It is presumed he died during this campaign, possibly during the disastrous siege of Damascus in 1148 or in subsequent engagements in the Holy Land, a common fate for many European knights who ventured east.

Cacciaguida's enduring legacy is overwhelmingly shaped by his prominent role in Canto XV of Dante's *Paradiso*, where he appears as a beatified soul in the Heaven of Mars. Through Cacciaguida, Dante not only traces his own lineage but also offers a powerful, idealized vision of 12th-century Florence: a city of civic virtue, simpler customs, and unwavering faith, starkly contrasted with the perceived corruption and factionalism of Dante's own time. He serves as a moral guide, prophesying Dante's exile and offering solace.

His literary resurrection cemented his image as the archetypal righteous crusader and noble ancestor, providing Dante with a powerful narrative device to critique contemporary society while exalting a bygone era of Florentine honor and piety, a vision that has profoundly influenced subsequent understandings of medieval Italian identity.
